Chapter 6: Where the Personal and Political Collide
You know, it’s easy to think of politics as something that happens far away—inside government buildings, on TV, or maybe in the hands of people with power. But, here’s the thing: for most of us, politics isn’t just out there somewhere. It’s woven right into the fabric of our everyday lives, showing up in moments so small, we barely even notice. That line between what’s personal and what’s political? It’s a lot blurrier than we might think.
Imagine this: a parent at a playground, quietly watching their child try to fit in with a group of kids. They see how the boys are taking up all the space, how the girls are expected to be quiet, and how a child who doesn’t quite fit in gets left out. The parent wants to step in, to make things fair—but worries about being seen as “that parent.” Funny thing is, the rules of the playground aren’t written anywhere, but everybody seems to know what they are. And those same rules? They show up later in offices, in classrooms, even in the stories we hear about who gets to lead and who’s supposed to follow.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our private lives are shaped by public forces. Think about it: the way a woman is treated at work, or how a trans kid is welcomed—or left out—at school. Even those dinner table conversations about race. All of these are political acts, even when they don’t feel that way. The stories we grow up with about what’s normal, what’s possible, or what’s right—those aren’t just personal opinions. They’re shaped by laws, by the media, by choices that people in power make every single day.
Sometimes, the collision between the personal and political hits hard and fast. A teenager comes out to their family and is met with silence, or maybe even worse. A worker speaks up for better pay and is told to just be grateful for what they have. In those moments, it’s impossible not to see it—the personal is never just personal. The rules that shape our lives are bigger than any one of us, but they get enforced in the most intimate, everyday ways.
But here’s where it gets powerful. When we start to recognize this connection—when we realize our struggles aren’t just our own, but part of a bigger pattern—something shifts. Suddenly, it’s possible to imagine real change. A parent who speaks up at the playground, a worker who refuses to stay silent, a friend who calls out a cruel joke—these might seem like small acts, but they’re political, even if they don’t look like it on the surface.
Most people want to believe they’re in control of their own story. But the truth? We’re all shaped by forces we can’t always see. The good news is, by paying attention to these patterns—and by refusing to accept them as unchangeable—we can actually start to shift them. The personal and the political aren’t two separate worlds. They’re really just two sides of the same story.
